title: Causes of Sorrow and Anger
english: One struggles to encounter them. Indeed, desire rules over every pleasure, but sensation gives birth to desire; for what is without sensation is free from passion. For recluses the demons wrestle naked, but for those working out virtue in communities or companies they arm the less attentive of the brothers; and the second war is much lighter than the first, because it is not possible to find on earth men more bitter than demons, or all at once receiving their malice.

Concerning the eight logismoi: Eight are all the most general logismoi, in which every logismos is contained. First is that of gluttony, and after it that of fornication; third is that of avarice; fourth is that of sorrow; fifth is that of anger; sixth is that of acedia; seventh is that of vainglory; eighth is that of pride. Whether these all trouble the soul or do not trouble it is not up to us; but whether to let them linger or not, or to move passions or not to move them, is up to us.

The logismos of gluttony suggests a rapid fall to the monk of asceticism: picturing stomach and liver and spleen and dropsy, and a long disease, and scarcity of necessities, and helplessness of physicians. And it often brings him to the memory of certain brothers who have fallen into these passions. And there is a time when it even persuades him to compare those very sufferers with those exercising self-control, and to recount their own misfortunes, and how from asceticism they have become such.

The demon of fornication compels to desire different bodies; and he stands against those exercising self-control more fiercely, so that, accomplishing nothing, they may give up; and defiling the soul he bends it down toward those activities, making it say certain words and again hear, as if the matter were seen and present. Avarice suggests long old age and weakness of hands for work, and famines to come and diseases to befall, and the bitterness of poverty, and how shameful it is to receive from others the things for need.

10 Sorrow sometimes occurs by deprivation of desires, and sometimes it follows anger. By deprivation of desires it occurs thus: certain thoughts, having gone before, lead the soul into the memory of house and parents and former way of life. And when they see it not resisting but following, and being poured out in the pleasures according to the mind, then taking it they baptize it in sorrow, as if the former things did not exist nor could any longer exist through the present life; and the wretched soul, as much as it was poured out upon the former thoughts, so much was it contracted upon the second ones, having been humbled.

11 Anger is the sharpest passion; for it is called a heating and movement of temper against the one who has done wrong or is thought to have done wrong; which all day long makes the soul savage, but especially in prayers snatches away the mind, mirroring the face of the one who caused the grief. And sometimes, lingering and changing into wrath, it provides disturbances by night, wasting of the body and paleness, and attacks of venomous beasts. These four things, happening after wrath, one might find accompanied by more thoughts.

12 The demon of acedia, who is also called the noonday demon, is the heaviest of all demons; and he stands over the monk around the fourth hour, and circles his soul until the eighth hour. And first he makes the sun appear slow-moving or motionless to behold, showing the day as fifty hours. Then he compels him to look constantly toward the windows and to leap out of the cell, to gaze at the sun how far it is from the ninth hour, and to look here and there whether any of the brothers comes. Furthermore, he instills hatred toward the place and toward life itself, and toward the work of the hands; and suggests that love has departed from among the brothers and there is no one encouraging; and if during those days someone has grieved the monk, the demon adds this too to the increase of hatred. And he leads him also and

title: On Temperance and the Passions
english: A desire for other places, in which the things for need are easily found and a more convenient and advancing craft is attained; and he adds that it is not possible to please the Lord in the present place; for everywhere, he says, the divine is to be worshipped. He connects this with the memory of one's own people and of the former way of life; and he traces out a long duration of life, bringing the labors of asceticism before the eyes; and he moves the whole so-called mechanism so that the monk, having abandoned the cell, may flee to the stadium. After this demon another demon does not immediately follow; but a certain peaceful state and unspeakable joy succeeds the soul after the struggle.

13 The thought of vainglory is extremely subtle, and stands beside those who succeed, wishing to publish their struggles readily and hunting the honors from men, fashioning crying demons and women being healed and a certain crowd touching his garments; and finally it predicts priesthood to him, and sets those seeking him at the doors; and how, were he unwilling, he will be led away a prisoner. And having thus made him hang in mid-air with empty hopes, it flies away, leaving him either to the demon of pride to tempt him, or to that of sorrow, which also brings upon him thoughts contrary to his hopes; and sometimes it even hands over to the demon of fornication the one who a little before was a prisoner and a holy priest.

14 The demon of pride becomes the procurer of a most severe fall for the soul; for it persuades it not to confess God as helper, but to think itself the cause of its successes, and to puff itself up against the brothers as if they were senseless, because they do not all know this about it. And anger and sorrow follow upon this, and the final evil: derangement and madness and a multitude of demons seen in the air.

15 Regarding the eight thoughts: Reading, wakefulness, and prayer steady the wandering mind; hunger, toil, and withdrawal wither the inflamed desire; psalmody, patience, and mercy calm the swirling thumos; and these become effective when done in proper times and measures; for the immeasurable and the untimely are short-lived, and the short-lived are rather harmful and not useful.

When our soul reaches for various foods, then let it be confined to bread and water so that it may become thankful, even for the bare morsel itself; for satiety desires various delicacies, but hunger counts satiety with bread to be blessedness.
The lack of water contributes greatly to temperance; and let the three hundred Israelites with Gideon who subdued Midian persuade you (Judges 7:7).

Just as for life and death to occur together in the same person is among impossibilities, so for love to coexist with money in someone is among impossibilities; for love is destructive not only of money but even of our fleeting life itself.

He who flees all worldly pleasures is a tower unapproachable to the demon of sorrow; for sorrow is deprivation of pleasure, whether present or expected. But it is impossible to drive away this enemy while we have any attachment to earthly things; for there he sets his snare and works sorrow where he sees us most inclined.
Anger and hatred increase thumos; but almsgiving and gentleness diminish the present one.

Let the sun not set upon our provocation, so that the demons, standing by at night, may not terrify the soul and make the mind more cowardly for the coming day toward the battle; for fearful phantasms naturally arise from the disturbance of thumos; and nothing else makes the mind such a deserter as disturbed thumos.

Whenever the irascible part of our soul, having seized a pretext, is disturbed, then the demons also suggest withdrawal to us as something good, so that we may not free ourselves from disturbance by resolving the causes of sorrow. But when the desiring part is heated, then again they make us, the humane ones, harsh, calling us harsh and wild, so that of bodies...

title: Endurance and the Demons of Acedia and Vainglory
english: Desiring, we encounter bodies. Whom we must not obey; but rather do the opposite.

Do not give yourself to the thought of anger, fighting in your mind against the one who caused grief; nor again imagine more pleasure for the thought of fornication; for the one darkens the soul, while the other calls the soul toward the burning of passion; both make your mind dirty. And imagining images even at the time of prayer and not offering a pure prayer to God, you immediately fall to the demon of acedia, who most especially leaps upon such states and tears the soul like a prey, like a dog.

It is the nature of thumos to fight with demons and to contend for any pleasure. Therefore the angels, suggesting to us spiritual pleasure and the blessedness from it, urge us to turn our thumos against the demons; but those others, dragging us toward worldly desires, force thumos to fight against humans contrary to nature, so that the mind, being darkened and falling away from knowledge, becomes a traitor to the virtues.

Take care of yourself lest you provoke any of the brothers to flee in anger, and you may not escape in your life the demon of sorrow, which always becomes a stumbling block to you at the time of prayer.
Gifts extinguish grudges; and let Jacob persuade you, who with gifts approached Esau, who had come out to meet him with four hundred. But we, being poor, let us satisfy the need at the table.

When we fall to the demon of acedia, then dividing the soul with tears, let us make the one part entreating and the other part being entreated, sowing good hopes for ourselves and chanting the holy David: Why are you so sorrowful, my soul, and why do you disquiet me? Hope in God, for I shall still praise him; the salvation of my face and my God.
It is not necessary during the time of trials to leave the cell, fashioning seemingly reasonable pretexts, but to remain within.

To stand firm, to endure, and to receive bravely all things that come, but to exclude entirely the demon of acedia, which being the heaviest above all, most especially makes the soul well-tested. For fleeing such struggles and being surrounded unskillfully teaches the mind to be cowardly and a deserter.

And our holy and most practical teacher said: Thus the monk must always prepare himself as if he were to die tomorrow, and again to use the body as if he were to live in it for many years. For the former, he says, cuts off the thoughts of acedia and prepares the monk more urgently; the latter preserves the body safe and always maintains its temperance equally.

It is difficult to escape the thought of vainglory; for what you do toward its destruction, this becomes for you a beginning of another vainglory. And not against every right thought of ours do the demons oppose, but these evils also occur according to the ways we have been qualified.

I recognized the demon of vainglory to be pursued by almost all among the demons, and shamelessly standing over the falls of those pursuing virtue, displaying to the monk a greatness of virtues. He who has touched knowledge and reaps the pleasure from it will no longer be persuaded by the demon of vainglory, even when bringing to him all the pleasures of the world; for what could he promise greater than spiritual contemplation? Insofar as we are without taste of knowledge, we eagerly work out the practical life, showing our purpose to God that we do all things for the sake of his knowledge.

Remember your former life and the ancient failings, and how, being passionate, by Christ's mercy you crossed over to dispassion, and how again you came out of the world which humbled you many times and often. And consider this for me too: who is the one guarding you in the desert, and who is the one driving away the demons gnashing their teeth against you? For such thoughts indeed produce humility, but they do not admit the demon of pride.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
